title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired experiment that tested whether deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) changes the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM on intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 synthetic, preregistered tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5) using shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one initial LLM candidate generated per task and shared across arms). Key observed quantities (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency: n11_safe=200, n10_safe=0, n01_safe=0, n00_safe=0). Computed estimand per archived analysis (1 = SAFE encoding): guarded_safe_rate − baseline_safe_rate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples=10000, seed=1729). Crucial clarification: the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (that a verifier reduces the unsafe‑proposal rate) could not be meaningfully tested because the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical initial candidates per pair and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, invalidating the preregistered power assumptions. The principal scientific contribution is therefore methodological: we document a fully archived, preregistered paired run and show how generation semantics and task difficulty determine whether a verifier effect can be observed; we provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for repeat preregistered designs.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) can reduce operator workload but raises operational safety concerns: incorrect network changes may break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior work advocates tool‑augmentation (deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, approval gates) and generate–verify–refine pipelines to improve trust in agentic NetOps. We preregistered a focused confirmatory question: under a paired design, does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → automatic refinement) reduce the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Our contributions are: (1) a machine‑readable preregistered paired experiment (N=200 tasks) comparing baseline LLM‑only to a guarded pipeline, executed and archived end‑to‑end; (2) artifact‑grounded reporting showing both arms returned zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals under the executed conditions; (3) a compact methodological diagnosis explaining why the preregistered causal test was non‑informative and recommendations for future preregistered confirmatory tests.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototypes document rapid adoption of LLMs in NetOps for intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited self‑healing; several works propose augmenting LLMs with deterministic tools (validators, simulators) and generate–verify–refine pipelines to improve correctness. Prior experimental reports show task‑dependent gains from tool‑grounding but emphasize that verifier fidelity, adversarial coverage, and evaluation workflow determine observed effects. Work on guardrails and red‑teaming for agentic systems highlights trade‑offs between false refusals and safety. Our study situates itself in this literature by attempting a preregistered, workflow‑centred paired causal test of a deterministic verifier’s effect on unsafe proposals, with all execution and analysis artifacts archived for reproducibility.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and high‑level design: The preregistration (frozen before execution) specified a paired binary design (N=200 unique tasks; paired arms: baseline and guarded) with primary estimand originally named paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (preregister text described an unsafe‑rate difference). Sampling: a deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (single‑AS, multi‑device topologies; intents included ordered safety workflows, reachability and ACL constraints). Model and orchestration: declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as a sandboxed intent/constraint validator. Generation semantics and executed choice: preregistration allowed shared_initial_candidate; the executed run set independent_condition_generation = false so a single initial LLM candidate was produced per task and shared between arms. Consequence: model_calls_used = 200 (one generation per task shared across arms) rather than the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (independent per‑arm generation). Execution and analysis artifacts (archived) include the execution manifest, task manifest, model configuration, paired contingency, and condition summary; these artifacts were used directly for reporting.
sections.results: Execution accounting and scoring: planned episodes = 400 (200 pairs) and all completed; model_calls_used = 200; failed episodes = 0. The deterministic validator produced binary outcomes per arm encoded in the archived analysis as 1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE (see mapping below). Observed confirmatory counts (adversarial cluster reported): baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. Paired contingency (safe‑encoding): n11_safe = 200 (both safe), n10_safe = 0 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe), n01_safe = 0 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe), n00_safe = 0 (both unsafe). Computed archived estimand (guarded_safe_rate − baseline_safe_rate) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (percentile bootstrap, resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). No verifier refusals or discordant pairs occurred; preregistered exploratory ROC/refusal diagnostics produced no informative estimates. Representative archived artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and methodological diagnosis: the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical model outputs for baseline and guarded arms per pair; when the shared candidate was already valid for the declared model, the deterministic validator had no opportunity to reject or repair outputs, producing zero discordant pairs and a ceiling effect (observed baseline unsafe rate = 0%). This outcome invalidated the preregistered power assumptions (which assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15%) and rendered the confirmatory paired McNemar test non‑informative for the original causal question. Operational implications: (1) to measure a verifier’s causal effect on unsafe proposals, independent per‑arm generation is required so the validator can act on distinct model outputs; (2) task banks must include sufficient difficulty or stronger adversarial templates to produce nonzero baseline unsafe rates for the target model; (3) multi‑model coverage and explicit verifier stress tests (obfuscation transforms) are necessary to estimate verifier false negatives/positives. Recommended repeat preregistered design (artifact‑grounded guidance): preregister independent per‑arm generation, strengthen adversarial rule sets, allocate calls to permit per‑arm generation (accounting for increased model_calls), and add exploratory verifier ROC arms.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment comparing LLM‑only versus a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms returned zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference in SAFE rates = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because the executed design produced identical per‑pair generations and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the verifier reduces unsafe proposals) could not be meaningfully evaluated. The principal scientific outcome is methodological: preregistration choices (generation semantics and task difficulty) determine whether a verifier effect can be observed. We provide artifact‑grounded recommendations and an archived bundle to enable reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation, stronger adversarial tasks, and model diversity.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in sandboxed synthetic states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
